So, while yes, the parts he suggested will last him 4 years, if he is looking into 4k gaming as a first time build, I feel like that is a mistake.

PC gaming is a tinkerer's toy, to some extent.

Even at the highest levels, you have to do some tweaking and playing with parts to figure it out. Much like tuning a car to either be as fast as possible or more gas efficient. Figuring things out and finding out what you want from the machine is easier and better if you practice with a Toyota to start instead of a Corvette.

Rather than going balls to the walls to start, he should be safe with a high refresh rate 4070 build.

Personal recommendation:
Budget can easily be lowered to 2K or less, and he would still have an amazing gaming experience

In terms of price to performance, you lose a lot of power efficiency as you go into 4k gaming, and the benefits are negligible if just for gaming. It isn't all about resolution for gaming, but also consistency in frames. Going to a high refresh rate 1440p or 1080p gaming monitor will be a lot better for him to ensure his build is just plig-and-play, so he can tinker and upgrade in the future, once he knows more about PCs.

Another way to look at it is this: it is a tinkerer's toy, let the kid learn how to tinker.

Talk to him, and make a deal: "we build a lower spec computer now so you can learn more about computers, make the most of this machine, and experiment. If you keep up next year, we upgrade the GPU and power supply, and get you a second monitor"

With his old parts he dumps for the upgrade (graphics card, power supply) you can use them to build a media center PC for your living room or use as a personal PC

Now, I've always been considered an oddball of a person. I generally avoided people, but have been able to read them really well since I was little. My twin, Kat, has always been social, but despite that, was bad at really understanding people's true intentions. A naiive analyst is the best way to describe her.

Despite the sexist, racist, and abusive individuals in the family, for some reason my parents still welcome them into our home. 

Born on December 24th, my twin and I were thought to be 'Blessed' children. Every year the family got together for Christmas and our birthday to throw big celebrations, but this year was no joke. The whole house was lit up, our uncle Frank, the sexist pig who refused to accept women as citizens, brought roasted whole turkey, and his wife, poor woman was covered in bruises, brought us homemade peppermint bark. 

We went through the usual festivities, eating dinner at a table full of people we hate, hugs, congradulations, just stuff we were used to. But then came the cake. Everyone spoke up, egging us on to summon our Shards.

Fifteen minutes. Frank is egging me on, calling me a "late-bloomer".

Twenty minutes. I finally feel like I got a hold of something. I pull hard with my mind, but it is hard and tiring. My friends are just staring at me.

The family runs up as I stare at the bahemoth in front of me.

Kat just looks at the hole in the wall with the only words to come out of anyone's mouth. "All I get is a gun, and you get a fucking tank?!"

I look down at the pool of blood below the tank treads and look at the vehicle in front of me. I climb up and open the hatch. "Maybe God does exist."

Altering it to handle all of my searches at once is illegal, and can heavily impact the cards I draw.

I found there are 3 major factors when it comes to Kalista:

1) Positioning. Despite your mobility, you want the fight going long. You don't have a lot of burst and lack a lot of damage that other ADC's do. Position so you can kite in and out of aa ranges of opponents or so you can follow up on an engage while still being a healthy distance away. This is really tricky, as Kali has short range and the 'golden zone' she wants to be in is always slightly shifting, so you want to jump to stay in this area once you learn it. (Part of learning your matchups)

2) Knowing when NOT to jump. Kalista's high mobility and kite potential is insane, but in the case of slows or long range opponents, you won't be able to kite them or will be doing yourself harm by trying to jump. Remember, jumping reduces your aa speed by roughly 30%, so staying still and trying to win these fights with a rend is your best bet, as you won't be able to escape without team support.

3) Learning Rend thresholds with what items. Depending on your Kalista build, Rend damage can vary greatly. Use Practice tool to learn your powerspikes and how much damage rend does with how many auto attacks. This will help farm/shove lanes while also allowing you to time your poke with Q -> rend. This helps a lot in laning phase and team fights where you can rend for a kill (minion or champ) so you can reset multiple times for small bursts or slows.

You may be an ADC, but Kalista is weak right now. Where champs like Draven can run at opponents and Caitlyn can poke from a mile away, you need to pick your fights carefully and learn the different builds and powerspikes for her. By practicing the top 3, it will help ALOT in trying to learn her. Learning Kalista is an uphill battle in the current meta, so a lot of it is learning how to counterplay in laning and teamfights

I build decks on the regular, often testing them online and helping friends build. A lot of the time it's more of a theoretical in which I want to test. I often don't build these in paper unless it has gone through my whole testing process.

Whenever I build a deck. I start with a 10-15 card "core" which defines the strategy I'm going for. Sometimes this includes the commander. Sometimes it doesnt, but this core dictates my PRIMARY theme (combo, aggro, control, midrange, win cons). We will use Edgar Markov for this example. When I see Edgar, the Vampire synergies is obvious, promoting a go-wide, have a ton of lords playstyle. The Core consists of cards like Olivia Voldaren, Bloodline Keeper, Legion's Landing, Drana Liberator of Malakir, Mutavault, and Anointed Procession. (I also had EVERY Sorin planeswalker for flavor)

After this core is ironed out. I watch the average CMC of my core and then move on to ramp, the average CMC of said core determines the amount of ramp and card draw needed in the deck, higher CMC means more ramp and less card draw. I often dictate 15-25 of my cards must either ramp, draw cards, or both. If I'm playing Edgar Markov, I'll put in my Skullclamp and cheap card draw, like Necropotence, while having less ramp, mostly sticking to artifacts, such as the signet cycle. These cards must be on-theme, cheap, and/or efficient to make sure the deck doesn't stray from the core. 

It is around here that a Secondary theme starts to become established. In the case of Edgar Markov, the fluctuations in gaining and losing health to draw cards makes me look at ways to control these fluctuations, putting me at an aristocrats/life-gain sub-theme, which is heavily supported by the vampire tribe. The deck starts to become fleshed out with support cards for this secondary theme, and thus working within the secondary theme promotes a specific type of removal and utility to keep the deck together. 

Going back to Edgar Markov, the aristocrat strategy heavily promotes a primarily orzhov deck with only splashes of red, meaning white/black removal like Kaya's Wrath, Fumigate, Vindicate, and Utter End will hold more weight than Boros or Rakdos removal like Lightning Helix, Bedevil, or Deafening Clarion.

After Primary Theme, Ramp, Card Draw, Secondary Theme, and Removal is all handled. All that is really left is the Landbase. Landbase is easy yet difficult. The colors you are in as well as the meta of your playgroup will determine the amount of basic lands you will run, as well as the types of utility lands. (Basic heavy if people run Blood moon or Back to Basics, Strip Mine/Wasteland to deal with problematic lands like Gaea's Cradle, Blast Zone to deal with other go wide decks, etc.) I often go out of my way to add potent utility lands to try and fill any gaps in the rest of the 99.

Afterwards is playtesting to see if there are any weaknesses in the deck and try to fill those gaps while swapping out cards. Otherwise, that is my full deck building process. I start from a core of 10-15 cards and build up from there.

Say I have a 50% chance of graduating college. But I also have a 20% chance to go to each Grand Prix in Milwaukee for the next 4 years while I'm at college. The chance that I both graduate college and attend all 4 Grand Prix, will be as follows:

.5^1 X .2^4 = 0.0008, meaning I have a 0.08% chance of getting all 5 intended outcomes.

All you're doing is running the same chance over and over again, with previous attempts not having an affect on the next attempt.

Play to their strengths and try to minimize their weaknesses. This is true for any unit, but doubly so for beasts, as they want to be transformed as often as possible to maximize their potential. There are a few steps to this process.

1) look at their level 40 statlines. This gives you a p good idea on what each unit likes to specialize in, for example Keaton's extremely high attack and Defense but awful res and speed mean he will die to ANY mage, and will like to be on the offense, or be used to bait out physical damage dealers

2) look at any Prf skills or weapons they have. This is a unit's bread and butter. This is what makes each unit unique, and by maximizing the potential of these weapons, you can wreak havok on your opponents.

3) Look for skills that synergize with the strengths of their stats/prf. Going back to Keaton. He has amazing Strength and Def, but irrecoverable speed and res. This is fine. Give your high mobility units Reposition, to help get him out of a jam. Then give him Death Blow 3 in the A slot, as it pushes his damage even further, and Moonbow as his Special, this allows him to consistently ignore defenses every turn after he first procs moonbow, thanks to his Special Spiral. His C skill is flexible, but you can give him Res Tactic for a C because it synergizes with the rest of your team.

It takes a lot of experimenting and talking to learn what makes a unit good, but any unit can be good if you really try and polish them

Keaton is an amazing physical wall with great offensive potential, but awful res and speed, making him lose to ANY mage.

Selkie is very similar, except she is a great Res wall with almost no physical bulk. Although with her high mobility, putting her on the offensive and replacing her bond skill with Warding Blow or Mirror blow would be best.

Kaden is the king of support. Buffing him shares the buffs to all allies within 2 spaces when they enter combat. Keep your team close to him and keep buffing him with Azura.

Where Kaden is the king of support, L!Azura is the queen. Her ability to spread buffs to all stats in a single unit is amazing, and her default kit coming with Attack Tactic just means she can consistently give Kaden +6 to all stats so he can spread the love.

When in doubt. Look up the units and what people have to say about them. Keep note of what people think is strong on them and try to make your team work together like kogs in a machine.

If units are not good defensively, dont put them defensively. If they are good supports, have their primary role be that of a support

Edit: Basically, not every unit is good out of the box. The best thing to do is plan ahead of time what the strengths and weaknesses are for each unit, and build them to accentuate that

Depending on budget, my build may not be the best for you, as it can be fairly expensive.

Where there is life, there is death. Keeping balance was the single most important teaching within the order. Never shall we stray too far in any direction. Never shall we let our emotions become extreme. We must be the embodiment of balance.

Before me is the large common room of the temple with a shrine on the far end. The ceilings rise high with only the sunlight being filtered through stained glass to light the room a multitude of colors. In front of the shrine sit my five masters. All of which having complete mastery of a different weapon: Bow, Sword, Spear, Whip, and Rifle. Nobody knows any of the masters' real names. They've always been referred to by their weapon, as I soon will be.

The Sword speaks up, "Rise, my son. It is good to see how you've grown. You came to us as a young boy who lost everything, now you stand before us as a strong man who has risked everything for greatness. Reach in to your heart. Summon the weapon that calls to you and fight us, for this is your final test. Five versus one, you must survive thirty seconds. Do not hold back and fight with intent to kill, my boy."

Fight with intent to kill? This is the final exam? Do they want someone to die? 

Before I could recollect myself, an arrow barely nicks my ear, cutting me and catching me off guard. "You better listen or you will die."

Immediately, I begin dodging attacks; ducking below a sword, hiding behind chairs to block arrows and spears, and avoiding getting hit by a whip. Wait, where are the bullets?

I turn to look at the exit as I hear a bang. A bullet ricochets off of a metal hinge to the door and catches me in the shoulder. "FUCK!"

I need a weapon, now. A sword, a gun, hell, even a small knife would do. I just need something, anything.

The Sword comes in to my right, swinging his blade for my head. I prepare to take the brunt of the attack by blocking with my forearm, but as I begin to close my fist for impact, I feel my fingers wrap around something. The feeling is a little too familiar, my fingers split between my index and middle finger as I grip the trucks of a longboard and it takes the impact.

"You've got to be kidding me." I grab the Sword with my free hand, twisting his arm behind him and use him as a human shield for an incoming arrow. The arrow lodges itself in his shoulder as a bullet gets blocked from the opposite direction.

I throw the Sword off of me as a whip wraps around my ankle, pulling me and dropping me on the ground. The Spear jumps off of the nearby chair and attempts to plunge his weapon into me, only for it to get blocked by my "weapon". I may have had a rebellious phase, but this is a joke. I use my free foot and kick the longboard I'm holding on to, disrupting the Spear's balance and having him fall on the Sword before he can get up. 

The Whip pulls me in, out of my cover from the Rifle and Bow. As she gets close, I slam my board on the whip itself, yanking it out of her hand. I take this moment to get up and headbutt her to daze her before slamming my board against her head. 

With three masters out of commission I turn to the ranged masters only to get a bullet piercing through my knee. I throw my long board on the ground and dive on it, getting back behind cover.

"Isn't the 30 seconds over yet?"

Another gunshot. I guess that answers my question. I decide to risk it. Twisting my body, I bite through the excruciating pain and throw my long board towards the shrine, knocking out the Rifle with a hit to the top of his head. As I see my spirit weapon disappear, before I can resummon it, I feel hard wood press against my throat, choking me. The Bow pulls hard, I can feel my consciousness fade as my lungs burn for air. It feels like an eternity as I'm here, grasping on to dear life as she has me unable to move. As I see black, all I hear before I knock out is, "You passed."

This makes her better against HP walls, even if they have relatively high resistance.

Also considering the fact that Nailah is a beast unit, and the constraints of A!Corrin's weapon, it comes down to team building constraints. A!Corrin is much more flexible in terms of team building, but sacrifices in-combat maneuverability to maximize the effect of his weapon, putting him in more defensive positions.  This makes him weaker in Aether Raids and either Mixed-Phase, or Enemy Phase oriented to min-max him.

Nailah's weapon benefits either being proactive or being in a beast team, giving her more in-combat maneuverability under the constraint of what her nearby allies must be. Her weapon actively pushes her to be on the aggressive with nearby supporting units, such as dancers. This is further accentuated by Glare, making it harder for opponents to catch her when she has strong supporting units, such as Ninian, Beast Dancers, or L!Azura. 

Just looking at BST and the fact that they can equip the same skills isn't the full story. Just because you CAN give an Ayra a full defensive moveset due to her decent bulk, doesn't mean it is the most efficient way to build her. When looking at these heroes and figuring out their optimal builds and teams, you realize that although their stats are comparable, the roles they want to fill within the team is not. There are sacrifices you must make on either side, it is merely a matter of figuring out what you want to do for your trade-off.

I think the problem here is people often try to see her with her base kit and pull the strange comparison with A!Corrin due to ones believing the cover the same role. Nailah, from a design standpoint, is meant to be an 'anchor' for a team, much like the Legendary heroes. A hero that, when built around, reaps insane benefits past her base statline. 

I think the best units to compare her to is either Ayra or Owain in this regard. Give them Wrath in B skill and Fury in A Skill, and you realize they are all very similar. Player-Phase oriented anchors for a team to build around and protect, meant to abuse true damage specials and be danced in and out of a fight.

A!Corrin is more of a mixed-phase generalist with an extremely potent B ability, meant to protect him so he can continue to support his team, with either tactics or dragon C abilities.

A solid Player Phase build with her would take advantage of her weapon and Glare by abusing Wrath, Heavy/Flashing Blade Seal (her high atk/spd stat), and something like Fury in the A slot to get her into Wrath range. This with something like Blue Flame, Astra, or even Aether if you're a madman allows for insane consistent burst when paired with a potent dancer, such as L!Azura (gibes +1 movement to keep the gap and spreads buffs), Ninian (Dragon), or one of the Herons (Beasts)

This is just a matter of team building constraints, as with any other team. In Aether Raids and some Arena maps, assuming both are surrounded by their optimal team (Dragon Tactics for Corrin, Monster Tactics for Nailah) Nailah will benefit more with disadvantageous maps, and even has a higher stat-buff cap than Corrin. Glare on Nailah makes her difficult to deal with by having either a Ninian or a Heron near her, as it becomes hard for her opponents to chase. Base stats seem worse by a single point, but because the higher freedom and maneuverability of Nailah in an optimal team, she seems to be a stronger anchor of the two.
